pos: n. (height, elevation; in the prophets the pride of man that the day of the LORD is appointed to bring down)
etymology: From lofty, of Scandinavian origin through loft, the air or an upper room. The Hebrew is gobah or rum, height — the same vocabulary used of mountains and towers, applied to the human heart.
biblical_def: “And the loftiness of man shall be bowed down, and the haughtiness of men shall be made low: and the LORD alone shall be exalted in that day” (Isaiah 2:17). The chapter is a sustained assault on human height. It begins: “The lofty looks of man shall be humbled, and the haughtiness of men shall be bowed down, and the LORD alone shall be exalted in that day” (Isaiah 2:11), and the middle of it lists what will be brought low — the cedars of Lebanon, the oaks of Bashan, the high mountains, every high tower, every fenced wall, the ships of Tarshish. The principle is stated flatly: “the day of the LORD of hosts shall be upon every one that is proud and lofty, and upon every one that is lifted up; and he shall be brought low” (Isaiah 2:12). Jeremiah applies the same charge to a nation: “We have heard the pride of Moab, (he is exceeding proud) his loftiness, and his arrogancy, and his pride, and the haughtiness of his heart” (Jeremiah 48:29) — five words for the same sin piled into one verse. The refrain of Isaiah 2 gives the reason God is set against height: the LORD alone shall be exalted in that day. There is one exaltation, and every rival is a trespass on it.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines loftiness as elevation in place or condition, and also pride, haughtiness, elevation of manner.
webster_full: LOFTINESS, n. Height; elevation in place or position.
2. Pride; haughtiness.
3. Elevation of attitude or mien; dignity.
4. Sublimity; elevation of diction or sentiment.
HAUGHTY, a. Proud and disdainful; having a high opinion of one's self, with some contempt for others.
scriptures: Isaiah 2:17
And the loftiness of man shall be bowed down, and the haughtiness of men shall be made low: and the LORD alone shall be exalted in that day.
Isaiah 2:11
The lofty looks of man shall be humbled, and the haughtiness of men shall be bowed down, and the LORD alone shall be exalted in that day.
Isaiah 2:12
For the day of the LORD of hosts shall be upon every one that is proud and lofty, and upon every one that is lifted up; and he shall be brought low:
Jeremiah 48:29
We have heard the pride of Moab, (he is exceeding proud) his loftiness, and his arrogancy, and his pride, and the haughtiness of his heart.
corruption_summary: Pride is reclassified as healthy self-regard and its opposite as a deficiency, so the sin Scripture attacks most persistently has no name left.
corruption_paragraphs: The therapeutic vocabulary of the last century performed a remarkable inversion: pride became a good to be cultivated and its lack a condition to be treated, while humility was recast as poor self-image. Isaiah 2 assumes the older and truer account. Loftiness is not a mood; it is a claim to a height that belongs to God alone, and the day of the LORD is appointed against it. Nothing in the chapter suggests that a low view of oneself is the goal — the goal is stated in the refrain, the LORD alone shall be exalted in that day. Humility in Scripture is not a man thinking badly of himself; it is a man thinking accurately about God, after which his own height ceases to be an interesting question.

The second thing usually missed in Isaiah 2 is how much of what is brought low is genuinely good. Cedars of Lebanon and oaks of Bashan are magnificent trees; ships of Tarshish were the achievement of an age. God is not against excellence, and Scripture praises skill, strength and beauty repeatedly. What He is against is height that has become a rival, and the list is there to show that no created greatness survives the comparison. Jeremiah's five-fold indictment of Moab — pride, loftiness, arrogancy, pride again, haughtiness of heart — is the same doctrine applied to a nation that had every natural reason for confidence.
roots_summary: Hebrew gobah, height or pride — Jeremiah 48:29; rum, to be high — Isaiah 2:11-17; gaon, pride, and gabhuth, haughtiness — the vocabulary of Isaiah 2.
roots_lines: Hebrew gobah — height, elevation, and hence pride; Jeremiah 48:29, of Moab's loftiness.
Hebrew rum — to be high, lifted up; Isaiah 2:12, of every one that is lifted up.
Hebrew shachach — to bow down, to be humbled; Isaiah 2:11, 2:17, what God does to loftiness.
Hebrew gaon — pride, excellency; Jeremiah 48:29, one of the five terms heaped on Moab.
Isaiah 2:22 closes the argument: cease ye from man, whose breath is in his nostrils: for wherein is he to be accounted of?
usage: “The loftiness of man shall be bowed down” — and the LORD alone exalted.
“Every one that is proud and lofty… shall be brought low” — the day of the LORD is against height.
Even the cedars and the ships are on the list; excellence is not the offence.

pos: adj. (stubbornly fixed, refusing to yield; used of Sihon whose heart God hardened, and of Israel whose brow was brass)
etymology: Latin obstinatus, from obstinare, to stand firm against. The Hebrew in Deuteronomy 2:30 is ammets, to make strong or firm; in Isaiah 48:4 qasheh, hard.
biblical_def: Both occurrences carry the same difficulty, and neither Testament flinches from it. The first is Sihon: “But Sihon king of Heshbon would not let us pass by him: for the LORD thy God hardened his spirit, and made his heart obstinate, that he might deliver him into thy hand, as appeareth this day” (Deuteronomy 2:30). Two things are asserted in one sentence — Sihon would not, and the LORD made his heart obstinate — and the purpose clause is God's. The next verse shows the outcome already granted: “Behold, I have begun to give Sihon and his land before thee” (Deuteronomy 2:31). The second is Israel: “Because I knew that thou art obstinate, and thy neck is an iron sinew, and thy brow brass” (Isaiah 48:4). God says He declared things beforehand precisely because He knew this about them, so that they could not credit their idols. Paul states the doctrine in a sentence: “Therefore hath he mercy on whom he will have mercy, and whom he will he hardeneth” (Romans 9:18). Obstinacy in Scripture is always genuinely the man's own, and never outside God's government.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines obstinate as stubborn, fixed in opinion or resolution, not yielding to reason, arguments or persuasion.
webster_full: OBSTINATE, a. Stubborn; pertinacious; fixed firmly in resolution or opinion; not yielding to reason, arguments or other means.
2. Not yielding or not easily subdued or removed; as an obstinate fever.
OBSTINACY, n. A fixedness in opinion or resolution that cannot be shaken; stubbornness.
HARDEN, v.t. To make hard or more hard; to confirm in wickedness, opposition or enmity.
STIFF-NECKED, a. Stubborn; inflexibly obstinate; contumacious.
scriptures: Deuteronomy 2:30
But Sihon king of Heshbon would not let us pass by him: for the LORD thy God hardened his spirit, and made his heart obstinate, that he might deliver him into thy hand, as appeareth this day.
Isaiah 48:4
Because I knew that thou art obstinate, and thy neck is an iron sinew, and thy brow brass;
Romans 9:18
Therefore hath he mercy on whom he will have mercy, and whom he will he hardeneth.
Deuteronomy 2:31
And the LORD said unto me, Behold, I have begun to give Sihon and his land before thee: begin to possess, that thou mayest inherit his land.
corruption_summary: The hardening texts are softened into permission, or pressed until God becomes the author of sin, and Scripture holds a line between the two.
corruption_paragraphs: The commonest evasion of Deuteronomy 2:30 is to read hardened as allowed to harden. The text does not permit it: the LORD hardened his spirit and made his heart obstinate, and the purpose was that Israel should possess the land. The same pattern governs Pharaoh, of whom Scripture says both that he hardened his own heart and that God hardened it, and Paul chooses that very case to answer the objection every reader raises — why doth he yet find fault? His reply is not an explanation but a rebuke: nay but, O man, who art thou that repliest against God? The doctrine of reprobation is not a Reformed invention; it is Romans 9, and the Confession states it in Scripture's own terms.

The opposite error presses the doctrine until God becomes the author of sin, which the Confession expressly denies and Scripture never says. Sihon would not let Israel pass; the refusal was his own, arising from his own heart, and he is nowhere excused by the hardening. God's decree establishes the reality of second causes rather than abolishing it. The pastoral use of this doctrine is the one Isaiah makes: God told Israel the future in advance because He knew their brow was brass, so that when it came to pass they could not say their idol had done it. Hardening is never information a man may use about himself — the warning to the reader is always today, if ye will hear his voice, harden not your hearts.
roots_summary: Hebrew ammets, to make firm or strong — Deuteronomy 2:30; qasheh, hard, stiff — Isaiah 48:4; Greek skleruno (G4645), to harden — Romans 9:18, Hebrews 3:8.
roots_lines: Hebrew ammets — to make strong, firm, obstinate; Deuteronomy 2:30, of Sihon's heart.
Hebrew qasheh — hard, severe, stiff; Isaiah 48:4, with the iron sinew and the brazen brow.
Hebrew chazaq — to strengthen, harden; the verb used repeatedly of Pharaoh in Exodus.
Greek skleruno (G4645) — to harden; Romans 9:18, and Hebrews 3:8, harden not your hearts.
Hebrews 3:13 gives the practical direction of the doctrine: exhort one another daily, lest any be hardened through the deceitfulness of sin.
usage: “Sihon… would not” and “the LORD thy God… made his heart obstinate” — both in one verse.
“Whom he will he hardeneth” — Paul's summary, and he anticipates the objection.
Hardening is never a man's information about himself; the word to him is today.

pos: adj. (strong, bold, proud; of the heart of the Assyrian, the look of the little horn, and words spoken against the LORD)
etymology: From Old French estout, bold or proud. The older English sense is arrogance rather than bulk. It renders Hebrew godel (greatness, of the stout heart), rab (great, of a look), and chazaq (strong, of words).
biblical_def: The word marks the sin God particularly answers: self-congratulation over borrowed power. Assyria is His rod, and He announces He will punish it: “I will punish the fruit of the stout heart of the king of Assyria, and the glory of his high looks” (Isaiah 10:12), because the king said “By the strength of my hand I have done it, and by my wisdom; for I am prudent” (Isaiah 10:13). Daniel uses it of the little horn: “that horn that had eyes, and a mouth that spake very great things, whose look was more stout than his fellows” (Daniel 7:20). Malachi turns it on the covenant people, and their reply is the most modern thing in the book: “Your words have been stout against me, saith the LORD. Yet ye say, What have we spoken so much against thee?” (Malachi 3:13). They do not know they have said anything. The next verse quotes them: “Ye have said, It is vain to serve God: and what profit is it that we have kept his ordinance” (Malachi 3:14). Job supplies the ordinary sense with no moral charge: “the stout lion's whelps are scattered abroad” (Job 4:11).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines stout as strong, lusty, valiant, bold, and in a bad sense proud, resolute or obstinate.
webster_full: STOUT, a. Strong; lusty; vigorous; robust; sinewy; muscular.
2. Bold; intrepid; valiant; brave.
3. Large; bulky.
4. Proud; resolute; obstinate; as in the phrase, to be stout against the LORD.
5. Firm; as a stout vessel.
scriptures: Malachi 3:13
Your words have been stout against me, saith the LORD. Yet ye say, What have we spoken so much against thee?
Isaiah 10:12

Wherefore it shall come to pass, that when the Lord hath performed his whole work upon mount Zion and on Jerusalem, I will punish the fruit of the stout heart of the king of Assyria, and the glory of his high looks.
Isaiah 10:13

For he saith, By the strength of my hand I have done it, and by my wisdom; for I am prudent: and I have removed the bounds of the people, and have robbed their treasures, and I have put down the inhabitants like a valiant man:
Malachi 3:14
Ye have said, It is vain to serve God: and what profit is it that we have kept his ordinance, and that we have walked mournfully before the LORD of hosts?
corruption_summary: Complaint against God is not recognised as speech against Him, and Malachi's congregation asks in genuine surprise what they have said.
corruption_paragraphs: Malachi 3:13 is the sharpest diagnostic in the Minor Prophets, because the accused do not recognise the charge. What have we spoken so much against thee? is asked in good faith. Then God quotes them, and the quotation is the ordinary grumbling of religious people who feel their obedience has not paid: it is vain to serve God, and what profit is it. No blasphemy was intended and none was noticed. This is how most speech against God is actually made — not in defiance but in disappointed accounting, by people who keep the ordinance and resent the terms. Scripture calls it stout words, and the church that only warns against overt unbelief will never name it.

Isaiah 10 supplies the doctrine of instruments, which is much needed and rarely taught. Assyria is God's rod, sent by Him against a hypocritical nation, and Assyria is then punished for the pride with which it swung. By the strength of my hand I have done it is the offence — not the conquest, which God ordained, but the credit taken for it. Every person and nation used by God to accomplish something is exposed to precisely this temptation, and the axe boasting against him that heweth with it is Isaiah's image for it two verses later. Success in a work God gave is the most reliable producer of a stout heart there is.
roots_summary: Hebrew godel, greatness — Isaiah 10:12; rab, great — Daniel 7:20; chazaq, strong — Malachi 3:13; shachal, a fierce lion — Job 4:11.
roots_lines: Hebrew godel — greatness, magnitude; Isaiah 10:12, of the stout heart of the king of Assyria.
Hebrew chazaq — strong, hard; Malachi 3:13, of words stout against the LORD.
Hebrew rab — great; Daniel 7:20, whose look was more stout than his fellows.
Hebrew shachal — a fierce or strong lion; Job 4:11, the one occurrence with no moral charge.
Isaiah 10:15 presses the point: shall the axe boast itself against him that heweth therewith?
usage: “Your words have been stout against me… Yet ye say, What have we spoken?”
“By the strength of my hand I have done it” — the offence of the instrument.
“A mouth that spake very great things, whose look was more stout than his fellows”.

pos: v.i. (to venture without warrant; used of Israel going up without the ark, of the prophet who speaks unsent, and of Haman's daring)
etymology: Latin praesumere, to take beforehand. To presume is to take what has not been given — a warrant, an office, a permission — and Scripture treats it as a distinct category of sin, separate from weakness.
biblical_def: After the spies' report and the sentence of forty years, Israel changed its mind and went to fight: “But they presumed to go up unto the hill top: nevertheless the ark of the covenant of the LORD, and Moses, departed not out of the camp” (Numbers 14:44). The detail is the point — the ark stayed behind, and so did Moses, and the army went anyway. “Then the Amalekites came down, and the Canaanites which dwelt in that hill, and smote them, and discomfited them” (Numbers 14:45). Doing the right thing a day late, without the command, is not obedience. The second use guards the prophetic office: “But the prophet, which shall presume to speak a word in my name, which I have not commanded him to speak, or that shall speak in the name of other gods, even that prophet shall die” (Deuteronomy 18:20), with the test following in verse 22 — if the thing follow not, the prophet hath spoken it presumptuously. The third is Ahasuerus asking after Haman: “Who is he, and where is he, that durst presume in his heart to do so?” (Esther 7:5). In every case the sin is acting on an authority that was never granted.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines presume as to venture without positive leave, to form confident opinions without sufficient evidence, and to make confident or arrogant attempts.
webster_full: PRESUME, v.t. To take or suppose to be true or entitled to belief, without examination or positive proof.
PRESUME, v.i. To venture without positive leave.
2. To form confident or arrogant opinions; with on or upon.
3. To make confident or arrogant attempts.
PRESUMPTUOUS, a. Bold and confident to excess; adventuring without reasonable ground of success.
scriptures: Numbers 14:44
But they presumed to go up unto the hill top: nevertheless the ark of the covenant of the LORD, and Moses, departed not out of the camp.
Deuteronomy 18:20
But the prophet, which shall presume to speak a word in my name, which I have not commanded him to speak, or that shall speak in the name of other gods, even that prophet shall die.
Numbers 14:45
Then the Amalekites came down, and the Canaanites which dwelt in that hill, and smote them, and discomfited them, even unto Hormah.
Deuteronomy 18:22

When a prophet speaketh in the name of the LORD, if the thing follow not, nor come to pass, that is the thing which the LORD hath not spoken, but the prophet hath spoken it presumptuously: thou shalt not be afraid of him.
corruption_summary: Speaking for God without a warrant carries a death sentence in Deuteronomy and no consequence at all in the modern church.
corruption_paragraphs: Deuteronomy 18:20 attaches capital punishment to presuming to speak a word in the LORD's name that He has not commanded, and verse 22 supplies a test anyone can apply: if it does not come to pass, the LORD did not say it. The contemporary market in personal prophecy operates in flat defiance of both. Words are delivered in God's name, they fail, and no one is held to anything — the failure is explained by the hearer's faith or by a shifted timetable. The cessationist position of the Reformed churches follows from the closed canon, but even those who expect continuing revelation have no way around the standard Moses set: God attaches His name to nothing that fails.

Numbers 14 addresses the subtler form, and it is the one that catches earnest people. Israel repented of their unbelief and set out to do the very thing God had originally commanded — and were destroyed, because the command had been withdrawn and the ark did not move. Zeal for a good work is not the same as a commission to do it, and Moses said plainly, go not up, for the LORD is not among you. A man may be doing something Scripture generally commends and still be presuming, if he is doing it in a place and hour where God has not sent him. The mark of the difference is usually visible in advance: the ark stayed in the camp.
roots_summary: Hebrew aphal, to swell or be presumptuous — Numbers 14:44; zud, to act proudly or presumptuously — Deuteronomy 18:20, 22; male leb, to fill the heart — Esther 7:5.
roots_lines: Hebrew aphal — to swell, to be lifted up; Numbers 14:44, of the presumption to go up.
Hebrew zud — to act proudly, presumptuously; Deuteronomy 18:20, 18:22, and the sin of presumptuous sins in Psalm 19:13.
Hebrew male leb — to fill the heart, hence to dare; Esther 7:5, who durst presume in his heart.
Hebrew Hormah — destruction; Numbers 14:45, the place the presumption ended.
Psalm 19:13 makes it a matter of prayer: keep back thy servant also from presumptuous sins; let them not have dominion over me.
usage: “They presumed to go up… nevertheless the ark… departed not out of the camp”.
“If the thing follow not… the prophet hath spoken it presumptuously” — a test anyone can apply.
Doing the right thing a day late, without the command, is not obedience.

pos: adj. (hasty, precipitate; forbidden of the mouth before God, and healed in the promised restoration)
etymology: From Middle English rasch, quick, of Germanic origin. The Hebrew in Ecclesiastes 5:2 is bahal, to be hasty or alarmed; in Isaiah 32:4 mahar, hasty, of a heart that will one day understand knowledge.
biblical_def: The command concerns worship and speech together: “Be not rash with thy mouth, and let not thine heart be hasty to utter any thing before God: for God is in heaven, and thou upon earth: therefore let thy words be few” (Ecclesiastes 5:2). The reason given is not that God dislikes speech but that the distance is very great — God is in heaven, and thou upon earth — and the conclusion drawn from His transcendence is brevity. The preceding verse sets the scene: “Keep thy foot when thou goest to the house of God, and be more ready to hear, than to give the sacrifice of fools” (Ecclesiastes 5:1). What follows is about vows: “When thou vowest a vow unto God, defer not to pay it; for he hath no pleasure in fools: pay that which thou hast vowed” (Ecclesiastes 5:4), and Proverbs warns of the same trap — “It is a snare to the man who devoureth that which is holy, and after vows to make enquiry” (Proverbs 20:25). Rashness is promising God in a moment of feeling what will have to be paid in a season of cost. Isaiah promises the cure: “The heart also of the rash shall understand knowledge, and the tongue of the stammerers shall be ready to speak plainly” (Isaiah 32:4).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines rash as hasty in council or action, precipitate, resolving or entering on a project without due deliberation.
webster_full: RASH, a. Hasty in council or action; precipitate; resolving or entering on a project or measure without due deliberation.
2. Uttered or undertaken with too much haste or too little reflection; as rash words; a rash undertaking.
3. Quick; sudden; as rash gunpowder.
RASHNESS, n. Too much haste in resolving or in undertaking a measure.
VOW, n. A solemn promise made to God, or by a pagan to his deity.
scriptures: Ecclesiastes 5:2
Be not rash with thy mouth, and let not thine heart be hasty to utter any thing before God: for God is in heaven, and thou upon earth: therefore let thy words be few.
Ecclesiastes 5:1
Keep thy foot when thou goest to the house of God, and be more ready to hear, than to give the sacrifice of fools: for they consider not that they do evil.
Ecclesiastes 5:4
When thou vowest a vow unto God, defer not to pay it; for he hath no pleasure in fools: pay that which thou hast vowed.
Isaiah 32:4
The heart also of the rash shall understand knowledge, and the tongue of the stammerers shall be ready to speak plainly.
corruption_summary: Volume and spontaneity in prayer are mistaken for fervour, and Ecclesiastes grounds brevity in the doctrine of God.
corruption_paragraphs: Ecclesiastes 5:2 makes an argument that runs directly against a great deal of contemporary practice: because God is in heaven and you are on earth, therefore let thy words be few. Brevity is deduced from transcendence. Much modern public prayer assumes the opposite — that length, spontaneity and emotional pitch are the marks of sincerity — and our Lord specifically warned against thinking we shall be heard for our much speaking. The Preacher is not commending coldness. He is saying that a man who has grasped who he is addressing will not chatter, and that the sacrifice of fools is offered by people who consider not that they do evil.

The vow passage is the practical edge and it lands hardest in emotionally charged settings. A rash vow is made in a moment of feeling and comes due later in the cold; Jephthah is the terrible example, and Proverbs 20:25 describes the man who devotes something holy and afterwards makes enquiry — that is, promises first and counts the cost afterward. The remedy Scripture gives is not the abolition of vows, which it commands be paid, but deliberation before making them. Isaiah 32:4 holds out the promise that the rash heart is not permanently rash: it shall understand knowledge, and the stammering tongue shall speak plainly. Grace makes deliberate men out of hasty ones.
roots_summary: Hebrew bahal, to be hasty or dismayed — Ecclesiastes 5:2; mahar, hasty — Isaiah 32:4; nadar, to vow — Ecclesiastes 5:4; Greek propetes (G4312), rash — Acts 19:36.
roots_lines: Hebrew bahal — to be hasty, alarmed, precipitate; Ecclesiastes 5:2, of the mouth before God.
Hebrew mahar — hasty, swift; Isaiah 32:4, the heart of the rash that shall understand knowledge.
Hebrew nadar — to vow; Ecclesiastes 5:4-5, better not to vow than to vow and not pay.
Greek propetes (G4312) — falling forward, rash; Acts 19:36, do nothing rashly, and 2 Timothy 3:4 of the heady.
Ecclesiastes 5:5 states the alternative plainly: better is it that thou shouldest not vow, than that thou shouldest vow and not pay.
usage: “Be not rash with thy mouth… therefore let thy words be few” — brevity deduced from transcendence.
“Be more ready to hear, than to give the sacrifice of fools”.
“The heart also of the rash shall understand knowledge” — the condition is not permanent.

pos: adj. (hateful, offensive; used of the Ammonites' insult to David's messengers and of an intolerable household in Proverbs)
etymology: Latin odiosus, from odium, hatred. The Hebrew in 1 Chronicles 19:6 is baash, to stink, to become offensive — a vivid figure; in Proverbs 30:23 senuah, hated or unloved.
biblical_def: David had sent messengers to comfort Hanun on the death of his father, and Hanun's counsellors persuaded him they were spies; he shaved them, cut off their garments, and sent them away. “And when the children of Ammon saw that they had made themselves odious to David, Hanun and the children of Ammon sent a thousand talents of silver to hire them chariots and horsemen out of Mesopotamia” (1 Chronicles 19:6). The order of events is instructive: they insulted an ally, recognised what they had done, and responded by hiring an army — thirty-two thousand chariots (1 Chronicles 19:7). Repentance was available and was never considered. The Proverbs use is domestic: among the four things for which the earth is disquieted (Proverbs 30:21) is “an odious woman when she is married; and an handmaid that is heir to her mistress” (Proverbs 30:23). The Hebrew there means hated or unloved, and the proverb observes what happens when someone long despised is suddenly given power — a pattern the wisdom books notice repeatedly and treat as a genuine social calamity rather than a moral failing in the person elevated.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines odious as hateful, deserving hatred, and also offensive or disgusting, exposed to hatred.
webster_full: ODIOUS, a. Hateful; deserving hatred.
2. Offensive to the senses; disgusting; as an odious sight; an odious smell.
3. Causing hate; invidious; as, to make a man odious.
4. Exposed to hatred; as, to render a man odious.
DISQUIET, v.t. To disturb; to deprive of peace, rest or tranquillity.
scriptures: 1 Chronicles 19:6

And when the children of Ammon saw that they had made themselves odious to David, Hanun and the children of Ammon sent a thousand talents of silver to hire them chariots and horsemen out of Mesopotamia, and out of Syriamaachah, and out of Zobah.
Proverbs 30:23
For an odious woman when she is married; and an handmaid that is heir to her mistress.
Proverbs 30:21
For three things the earth is disquieted, and for four which it cannot bear:
1 Chronicles 19:7

So they hired thirty and two thousand chariots, and the king of Maachah and his people; who came and pitched before Medeba. And the children of Ammon gathered themselves together from their cities, and came to battle.
corruption_summary: Recognising an offence is confused with repenting of it, and Ammon shows a nation doing the first and arming instead of the second.
corruption_paragraphs: 1 Chronicles 19:6 records one of the plainest failures of repentance in the histories. The Ammonites saw that they had made themselves odious — the recognition was complete and accurate — and their response was to spend a thousand talents of silver on mercenaries. Acknowledgment is not repentance. A man may see exactly what he has done, describe it accurately, and then commit every resource he has to defending the position rather than making it right. Hanun could have sent an apology and a gift after David's humiliated messengers; instead he hired thirty-two thousand chariots and lost them. The sequence — offend, recognise, fortify — is the ordinary shape of a hardened conscience.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the wisdom literature's realism about power suddenly given. Proverbs 30:23 is not a slur on unloved women or on servants; the same chapter admires the ants, the conies, the locusts and the spider, and Proverbs elsewhere honours the virtuous woman at length. The observation is about disquiet: someone long despised, handed authority without preparation, is a hard thing for a household to bear, and pretending otherwise helps nobody. Scripture is willing to say plain things about how households and societies actually go wrong, and it says them without malice toward the persons involved.
roots_summary: Hebrew baash, to stink, to become odious — 1 Chronicles 19:6, Genesis 34:30, Exodus 5:21; senuah, hated or unloved — Proverbs 30:23.
roots_lines: Hebrew baash — to stink, to be offensive; 1 Chronicles 19:6, and Exodus 5:21 where Israel's savour is made abhorred before Pharaoh.
Hebrew senuah — hated, unloved; Proverbs 30:23, and used of Leah in Genesis 29:31.
Hebrew ragaz — to be disquieted, agitated; Proverbs 30:21, of the earth under the four things.
Hebrew Hanun — the Ammonite king whose counsellors persuaded him David's messengers were spies.
2 Samuel 10:4 records the insult itself: he shaved off the one half of their beards, and cut off their garments in the middle.
usage: “They had made themselves odious to David” — seen clearly, and never repented of.
“Three things the earth is disquieted, and for four which it cannot bear”.
Acknowledgment is not repentance; Ammon acknowledged and hired chariots.

pos: n. (a curse; specifically, a people whose name becomes the form of words others use when cursing)
etymology: Latin execratio, from exsecrari, to curse. The Hebrew alah is an oath or curse, and the sense here is technical: to become an execration is to have one's name used as the pattern for a curse.
biblical_def: Jeremiah warns the remnant against going down to Egypt: “so shall my fury be poured forth upon you, when ye shall enter into Egypt: and ye shall be an execration, and an astonishment, and a curse, and a reproach; and ye shall see this place no more” (Jeremiah 42:18). They went, and the sentence was repeated: “they shall even be consumed by the sword and by the famine: they shall die, from the least even unto the greatest… and they shall be an execration, and an astonishment, and a curse, and a reproach” (Jeremiah 44:12). Four nouns describe one fate, and the first is the most chilling. To become an execration is not merely to be cursed but to become the words — the byword others reach for when they wish evil on someone. The people who were called to be a blessing to all the families of the earth end as the standard form of a curse. Jeremiah adds that escape will be almost total in its absence: “none shall return but such as shall escape” (Jeremiah 44:14). The tragedy is that they had asked Jeremiah for the word of the LORD and promised to obey it, and then did the opposite.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines execration as a cursing, a curse pronounced, and imprecation of evil.
webster_full: EXECRATION, n. The act of cursing; a curse pronounced; imprecation of evil.
EXECRATE, v.t. To curse; to denounce evil against, or to imprecate evil on.
BYWORD, n. A common saying; a proverb; a term of reproach.
REPROACH, n. Censure mingled with contempt; abusive language.
ASTONISHMENT, n. Amazement; confusion of mind from fear, surprise or admiration.
scriptures: Jeremiah 42:18

For thus saith the LORD of hosts, the God of Israel; As mine anger and my fury hath been poured forth upon the inhabitants of Jerusalem; so shall my fury be poured forth upon you, when ye shall enter into Egypt: and ye shall be an execration, and an astonishment, and a curse, and a reproach; and ye shall see this place no more.
Jeremiah 44:12

And I will take the remnant of Judah, that have set their faces to go into the land of Egypt to sojourn there, and they shall all be consumed, and fall in the land of Egypt; they shall even be consumed by the sword and by the famine: they shall die, from the least even unto the greatest, by the sword and by the famine: and they shall be an execration, and an astonishment, and a curse, and a reproach.
Jeremiah 44:14

So that none of the remnant of Judah, which are gone into the land of Egypt to sojourn there, shall escape or remain, that they should return into the land of Judah, to the which they have a desire to return to dwell there: for none shall return but such as shall escape.
Deuteronomy 25:19

Therefore it shall be, when the LORD thy God hath given thee rest from all thine enemies round about, in the land which the LORD thy God giveth thee for an inheritance to possess it, that thou shalt blot out the remembrance of Amalek from under heaven; thou shalt not forget it.
corruption_summary: Guidance is sought from God with the decision already made, and Jeremiah 42 records what that costs.
corruption_paragraphs: The chapter around this word is the most exact account in Scripture of insincere enquiry. The remnant came to Jeremiah, asked him to pray, and swore that whether the answer was good or evil they would obey. They waited ten days for the word. It came, it told them to stay, and they immediately accused Jeremiah of lying and went to Egypt. The pattern is common and it is not confined to nations: guidance is sought after the decision has been taken, and the answer is tested against the decision rather than the decision against the answer. What made their case so grave was the oath. They had bound themselves in advance to obey a word they had not yet heard, and then refused it.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is what the sentence actually names. Israel was called in Abraham so that in him all families of the earth should be blessed, and a covenant people who abandon their calling do not become neutral — they become an execration, the form of words others use to curse. That is the trajectory of a church as well as a nation. A congregation exists to be a blessing in its place; when it is not, it does not simply fade quietly but becomes a byword in the community it was sent to serve, and every reader will know an instance.
roots_summary: Hebrew alah, an oath or curse — Jeremiah 42:18, 44:12; joined with shammah (astonishment), qelalah (a curse) and cherpah (reproach) in the fourfold sentence.
roots_lines: Hebrew alah — an oath, an imprecation; rendered execration in Jeremiah 42:18 and 44:12.
Hebrew shammah — astonishment, horror; the second term of the fourfold sentence.
Hebrew qelalah — a curse; the third, and the counterpart of the blessing promised to Abraham.
Hebrew cherpah — reproach, disgrace; the fourth term.
Jeremiah 42:5-6 records the oath they broke: the LORD be a true and faithful witness between us, whether it be good, or whether it be evil, we will obey.
usage: “Ye shall be an execration, and an astonishment, and a curse, and a reproach”.
To become an execration is to become the words others curse with.
They swore to obey the answer before they heard it, and refused it when it came.

pos: adj. (halting or unintelligible in speech; in Isaiah the foreign tongue that becomes a sign of judgment on those who would not hear plain words)
etymology: From stammer, Old English stamerian, to stutter. The Hebrew laeg in Isaiah 28:11 means mocking or barbarous speech — language that sounds like nonsense to the hearer, not a speech impediment in the speaker.
biblical_def: Isaiah is answering drunken priests and prophets who had mocked his preaching as baby-talk — precept upon precept, line upon line, here a little and there a little. His reply is a sentence of judgment: “For with stammering lips and another tongue will he speak to this people” (Isaiah 28:11). Since they would not hear the prophet's plain Hebrew, God would address them in Assyrian — the speech of an invading army, unintelligible and terrifying. The tragedy is stated in the next verse: “To whom he said, This is the rest wherewith ye may cause the weary to rest; and this is the refreshing: yet they would not hear” (Isaiah 28:12). Rest was offered in words they understood and refused; judgment came in words they could not understand. Isaiah repeats the figure later: “Thou shalt not see a fierce people, a people of a deeper speech than thou canst perceive; of a stammering tongue, that thou canst not understand” (Isaiah 33:19). Paul cites the passage in the tongues controversy at Corinth: “In the law it is written, With men of other tongues and other lips will I speak unto this people; and yet for all that will they not hear me, saith the Lord” (1 Corinthians 14:21).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines stammering as speaking with stops or hesitation, and to stammer as to stop in speaking or to speak with involuntary breaks.
webster_full: STAMMERING, ppr. Speaking with stops or difficulty; hesitating.
STAMMER, v.i. To stop in uttering syllables or words; to hesitate or falter in speaking.
BARBAROUS, a. Foreign; in the Greek sense, a foreigner, one who speaks a language not understood.
UNINTELLIGIBLE, a. That cannot be understood.
REFRESHING, n. Refreshment; relief after fatigue or suffering.
scriptures: Isaiah 28:11
For with stammering lips and another tongue will he speak to this people.
Isaiah 28:12
To whom he said, This is the rest wherewith ye may cause the weary to rest; and this is the refreshing: yet they would not hear.
1 Corinthians 14:21
In the law it is written, With men of other tongues and other lips will I speak unto this people; and yet for all that will they not hear me, saith the Lord.
Isaiah 33:19
Thou shalt not see a fierce people, a people of a deeper speech than thou canst perceive; of a stammering tongue, that thou canst not understand.
corruption_summary: Isaiah 28:11 is quoted as a promise of tongues-speaking, when Paul cites it in the same chapter where he uses it to restrain the practice.
corruption_paragraphs: 1 Corinthians 14:21 is regularly produced as scriptural warrant for tongues in the assembly. Paul's use of it runs the other way. He quotes Isaiah's sentence of judgment and draws the conclusion in the very next verse: tongues are for a sign, not to them that believe, but to them that believe not. His whole argument in the chapter is for intelligibility — five words with understanding are worth more than ten thousand in an unknown tongue — and he grounds it in a passage where unintelligible speech was a curse on a people who would not hear. Whatever a reader concludes about the continuance of the gift, quoting this verse in favour of unrestrained tongues reverses the argument of the apostle who quoted it first.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is Isaiah 28:12, one of the saddest verses in the prophets. God had spoken plainly, and what He said was this is the rest… this is the refreshing — and they would not hear. The judgment of unintelligible speech was measured to the refusal: they had called the prophet's clear words infantile babbling, and God gave them real babbling from an army. There is a warning here for congregations that find plain preaching dull. Clarity offered and despised is not a neutral event, and God has more than one way of speaking to a people who will not hear the first.
roots_summary: Hebrew laeg, mocking or barbarous speech — Isaiah 28:11; illeg, stammering — Isaiah 32:4; amoq saphah, deep of lip — Isaiah 33:19; Greek heteroglossos (G2084) — 1 Corinthians 14:21.
roots_lines: Hebrew laeg — mocking, stammering, barbarous; Isaiah 28:11, of the foreign tongue God would use.
Hebrew illeg — stammering; Isaiah 32:4, where the stammerer shall speak plainly in the restoration.
Hebrew amoq saphah — deep of lip, of speech too deep to perceive; Isaiah 33:19.
Greek heteroglossos (G2084) — of another tongue; 1 Corinthians 14:21, its only occurrence.
1 Corinthians 14:22 draws Paul's own conclusion: tongues are for a sign, not to them that believe, but to them that believe not.
usage: “With stammering lips and another tongue will he speak to this people” — a sentence, not a promise.
“This is the rest… yet they would not hear” — clarity offered and despised.
They called plain preaching baby-talk, and God sent them an army they could not understand.

pos: v. (taken unawares, seized suddenly; used of fear seizing hypocrites and of fortified cities taken without warning)
etymology: From Old French surprendre, to overtake or seize. The older English sense is military — a city is surprised when it is captured before it can shut its gates — and Scripture uses it that way for both cities and consciences.
biblical_def: The most searching use is inward: “The sinners in Zion are afraid; fearfulness hath surprised the hypocrites. Who among us shall dwell with the devouring fire? who among us shall dwell with everlasting burnings?” (Isaiah 33:14). Fear takes them the way a raiding party takes a town — suddenly, from within their own security, and among people who thought their place in Zion settled the matter. The other uses are literal and military. Moab: “Kerioth is taken, and the strong holds are surprised, and the mighty men's hearts in Moab at that day shall be as the heart of a woman in her pangs” (Jeremiah 48:41). And Babylon, the greatest fortress of the age: “How is Sheshach taken! and how is the praise of the whole earth surprised! how is Babylon become an astonishment among the nations!” (Jeremiah 51:41), with the figure of the sea coming up over her (Jeremiah 51:42). In each case the point is the same: what was thought impregnable was taken before it could react. Isaiah's answer to the surprised hypocrites is not escape but a description of a man who can dwell with the fire (Isaiah 33:15).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines surprise as to fall or come upon suddenly and unexpectedly, and to take unawares, especially of an enemy or a place.
webster_full: SURPRISE, v.t. To fall or come upon suddenly and unexpectedly; to come upon unawares.
2. To strike with wonder or astonishment by something sudden, unexpected or remarkable.
3. To confuse; to throw the mind into disorder by something suddenly presented.
SURPRISE, n. The act of coming upon unawares, or of taking suddenly and without preparation.
STRONGHOLD, n. A fastness; a fort; a fortified place; a place of security.
scriptures: Isaiah 33:14
The sinners in Zion are afraid; fearfulness hath surprised the hypocrites. Who among us shall dwell with the devouring fire? who among us shall dwell with everlasting burnings?
Jeremiah 51:41
How is Sheshach taken! and how is the praise of the whole earth surprised! how is Babylon become an astonishment among the nations!
Jeremiah 48:41
Kerioth is taken, and the strong holds are surprised, and the mighty men's hearts in Moab at that day shall be as the heart of a woman in her pangs.
Jeremiah 51:42
The sea is come up upon Babylon: she is covered with the multitude of the waves thereof.
corruption_summary: Assurance is grounded in religious position rather than in Christ, so that the fear which surprises the hypocrite is exactly the fear no one expects.
corruption_paragraphs: Isaiah 33:14 locates the hypocrites in Zion. They are inside the covenant community, not outside it, and their terror arrives without warning because their standing had never been examined. This is the danger of a religion of position: baptised, enrolled, present, orthodox in profession, and never once put to the question. The surprise in the verse is not that judgment came but that it came for them. The Puritan practice of self-examination, which modern churches have largely abandoned as morbid, existed to prevent exactly this — not to unsettle believers but to keep the merely religious from discovering their condition too late to do anything about it.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that no stronghold is a stronghold. Kerioth was taken; Babylon, the praise of the whole earth, was surprised in a night while her king was at a feast. The confidence of a fortified position is precisely what makes a surprise possible, since a city that expects an attack shuts its gates. Scripture's counsel to the believer is therefore not to build a stronger wall but to be found watching, and its comfort is that the day overtakes as a thief only those who are of the night. The children of light are not surprised.
roots_summary: Hebrew achaz, to seize or take hold — Isaiah 33:14; taphas, to capture — Jeremiah 48:41, 51:41; Sheshach, a cryptic name for Babylon.
roots_lines: Hebrew achaz — to grasp, seize, take hold of; Isaiah 33:14, of fearfulness seizing the hypocrites.
Hebrew taphas — to catch, capture; Jeremiah 48:41 and 51:41, of the strongholds taken.
Hebrew Sheshach — a cipher for Babylon; Jeremiah 25:26 and 51:41.
Hebrew chaneph — profane, hypocrite; Isaiah 33:14, of the sinners in Zion.
1 Thessalonians 5:4 gives the New Testament counterpart: ye, brethren, are not in darkness, that that day should overtake you as a thief.
usage: “Fearfulness hath surprised the hypocrites” — and they are in Zion.
“How is the praise of the whole earth surprised!” — Babylon taken in a night.
A city that expects an attack shuts its gates; the confident one does not.

pos: n. and adj. (the last in order or march; the position Dan held in the camp, and the stragglers Amalek attacked)
etymology: From hind, at the back, with the superlative -most. The Hebrew in Deuteronomy 25:18 is zanab, to cut off the tail — the verb itself means to attack the rear.
biblical_def: In the order of the camp the position was an honourable charge: “All they that were numbered in the camp of Dan were an hundred thousand and fifty and seven thousand and six hundred. They shall go hindmost with their standards” (Numbers 2:31) — the rearguard of a nation on the march. Amalek attacked precisely there, and God did not forget it: “How he met thee by the way, and smote the hindmost of thee, even all that were feeble behind thee, when thou wast faint and weary; and he feared not God” (Deuteronomy 25:18). Every clause is an aggravation — the hindmost, the feeble, the faint and weary — and the verdict is that he feared not God. The sentence follows: “thou shalt blot out the remembrance of Amalek from under heaven; thou shalt not forget it” (Deuteronomy 25:19). Joshua uses the term tactically in the pursuit at Beth-horon: “pursue after your enemies, and smite the hindmost of them; suffer them not to enter into their cities” (Joshua 10:19). The rear of a column is where the weak walk, and Scripture judges a people by what they do there.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines hindmost as the last, or that is in the rear of all others, and rear as the part of an army which is behind the rest.
webster_full: HINDMOST, a. The last; that is in the rear of all others.
HIND, a. Backward; pertaining to the part which follows.
REAR, n. The part of an army which is behind the other, either in marching or in a camp.
STRAGGLE, v.i. To wander from the direct course or way; to rove.
FEEBLE, a. Weak; destitute of much physical strength.
scriptures: Deuteronomy 25:18
How he met thee by the way, and smote the hindmost of thee, even all that were feeble behind thee, when thou wast faint and weary; and he feared not God.
Deuteronomy 25:19

Therefore it shall be, when the LORD thy God hath given thee rest from all thine enemies round about, in the land which the LORD thy God giveth thee for an inheritance to possess it, that thou shalt blot out the remembrance of Amalek from under heaven; thou shalt not forget it.
Numbers 2:31
All they that were numbered in the camp of Dan were an hundred thousand and fifty and seven thousand and six hundred. They shall go hindmost with their standards.
Joshua 10:19
And stay ye not, but pursue after your enemies, and smite the hindmost of them; suffer them not to enter into their cities: for the LORD your God hath delivered them into your hand.
corruption_summary: Strength is measured by what a people can achieve at the front, and Scripture measures it by what happens at the back of the column.
corruption_paragraphs: Deuteronomy 25:18 is one of the most morally precise sentences in the law. It does not merely say Amalek attacked Israel; it says he attacked the hindmost, the feeble, those who were behind because they could not keep up, and it does so when the nation was faint and weary. The concluding clause supplies the theology: and he feared not God. Preying on the weakest is treated as the definitive evidence of atheism in practice, whatever a people professes. That is a standard worth applying widely, and it applies to institutions as readily as to nations: the treatment of those at the back of the column, who can neither reward nor retaliate, is the reliable index of whether God is feared in a place.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the honour of the rearguard. Dan went hindmost with their standards as an appointed charge, because the rear of a marching nation is where the weak, the sick, the children and the aged are, and the largest tribes were placed to defend them. That is the pattern a church should recognise: the strongest are stationed where the slowest are. Congregations naturally organise around their most capable and visible members and let the back of the column fend for itself — which leaves precisely the people Amalek attacked precisely where Amalek found them.
roots_summary: Hebrew zanab, to cut off the rear — Deuteronomy 25:18, Joshua 10:19; acharon, hindmost, last — Numbers 2:31; chashal, feeble — Deuteronomy 25:18.
roots_lines: Hebrew zanab — from zanab, a tail; to attack the rear; Deuteronomy 25:18 and Joshua 10:19.
Hebrew acharon — hindmost, latter, last; Numbers 2:31, of the camp of Dan.
Hebrew chashal — feeble, faltering; Deuteronomy 25:18, its only occurrence, of those behind.
Hebrew Amalek — the nation whose remembrance was to be blotted out; Exodus 17:8-16, Deuteronomy 25:17-19.
Exodus 17:16 records the standing sentence: the LORD hath sworn that the LORD will have war with Amalek from generation to generation.
usage: “Smote the hindmost of thee, even all that were feeble behind thee” — and he feared not God.
“They shall go hindmost with their standards” — the rearguard as an appointed charge.
The treatment of the back of the column is the index of whether God is feared.
